title: Reproduction in Vertebrates

standard_text: Reproductive strategies in vertebrates: external and internal fertilisation; ovipary, ovovivipary and vivipary; the amniotic egg; precocial and altricial development; parental care. (summary of CAPS Life Sciences, Grade 12, Life Sciences: Reproduction in vertebrates)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Life Sciences worksheets (CAPS): external and internal fertilisation, ovipary, ovovivipary, vivipary, amniotic eggs and parental care. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Internal fertilisation is an adaptation to life on land.
body_html:
How to think about it

Fertilisation is external in most fish and amphibians (in water) and internal in reptiles, birds and mammals. Oviparous animals lay eggs that develop outside the body; ovoviviparous animals keep the eggs inside until they hatch; viviparous animals (most mammals) feed the embryo through a placenta and give birth to live young.

Reptiles and birds lay amniotic eggs with a shell, amnion, yolk sac, allantois and chorion that protect the embryo on land. Precocial young (antelope calves, chicks) can move soon after birth; altricial young (kittens, many songbirds) are helpless and need care. Animals that give more parental care produce fewer young.

Example

Which type of development does a springbok calf show?

It runs within hours.

Answer: precocial

Example

Which membrane in an egg stores waste?

Not the amnion

Answer: the allantois

Common mistakes

  • Thinking all reptiles lay eggs (some are ovoviviparous).
  • Mixing up ovipary and vivipary.
  • Thinking fish give a lot of parental care.

faq.q: Why do frogs lay so many eggs?
faq.a: Fertilisation is external and there is little care, so most eggs and tadpoles are lost.

faq.q: What is the advantage of the amniotic egg?
faq.a: The embryo develops in fluid, protected from drying out, so reptiles and birds could breed on land.

items.q: What is the job of the petals in a flower?
c: to hold the ovules that become seeds
to attract insects with colour and scent
to catch pollen on its sticky top
items.e: The job of the petals is to attract insects with colour and scent.

items.q: “The pollen joins with an ovule in the ovary (fertilisation).” What happens next?
c: The seeds are dispersed and can grow into new plants.
A bee visits a flower and pollen sticks to its body.
The ovule grows into a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
The bee carries the pollen to another flower of the same kind.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to join the stigma to the ovary?
items.e: The job of the style is to join the stigma to the ovary.

items.q: What is the role of the inner cell mass?
c: the outer layer of the blastocyst that attaches to the uterus
the cells of the blastocyst that form the embryo
the mature follicle that releases the ovum
items.e: Inner cell mass: the cells of the blastocyst that form the embryo.

items.q: “Pollen lands on the sticky stigma (pollination).” What happened just before?
c: The pollen joins with an ovule in the ovary (fertilisation).
The ovule grows into a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.
The bee carries the pollen to another flower of the same kind.
A bee visits a flower and pollen sticks to its body.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal.

items.q: Why do fish and frogs produce very many eggs?
c: most eggs are not fertilised or are eaten, so many are needed for some to survive
the parents look after each egg
they reproduce only once in a lifetime
items.e: External fertilisation and little parental care mean a high loss of eggs.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to make pollen?
items.e: The job of the anther is to make pollen.

items.q: “The pollen joins with an ovule in the ovary (fertilisation).” What happened just before?
c: Pollen lands on the sticky stigma (pollination).
A bee visits a flower and pollen sticks to its body.
The bee carries the pollen to another flower of the same kind.
The seeds are dispersed and can grow into new plants.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal.

items.q: Which cell or structure is responsible for making progesterone after ovulation?
items.e: Corpus luteum: making progesterone after ovulation.

items.q: Which cell or structure is responsible for holding enzymes that help the sperm enter the ovum?
items.e: Acrosome: holding enzymes that help the sperm enter the ovum.

items.q: What is the job of the anther in a flower?
c: to hold the ovules that become seeds
to attract insects with colour and scent
to catch pollen on its sticky top
items.e: The job of the anther is to make pollen.

items.q: Which cell or structure is responsible for nourishing the developing sperm?
items.e: Sertoli cells: nourishing the developing sperm.

items.q: What is the role of the placenta?
c: exchanging food, oxygen and wastes between mother and foetus
the mature follicle that releases the ovum
items.e: Placenta: exchanging food, oxygen and wastes between mother and foetus.

items.q: Which part of a flower has this job: to protect the flower when it is a bud?
items.e: The job of the sepals is to protect the flower when it is a bud.

items.q: In which group of animals is external fertilisation most common?
items.e: These animals reproduce in water, where sperm can swim to the eggs.

items.q: “A bee visits a flower and pollen sticks to its body.” What happens next?
c: The pollen joins with an ovule in the ovary (fertilisation).
Pollen lands on the sticky stigma (pollination).
The seeds are dispersed and can grow into new plants.
The bee carries the pollen to another flower of the same kind.
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal.

items.q: A frog lays its eggs in water, where a male fertilises them. What type of fertilisation is this?
items.e: Fertilisation happens outside the female's body.

items.q: “The ovule grows into a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.” What happens next?
c: The bee carries the pollen to another flower of the same kind.
The pollen joins with an ovule in the ovary (fertilisation).
The seeds are dispersed and can grow into new plants.
Pollen lands on the sticky stigma (pollination).
items.e: Pollination → fertilisation → seed and fruit → dispersal.

items.q: Why is internal fertilisation an advantage on land?
c: gametes do not dry out and more eggs are fertilised
items.e: The sperm swims in fluids inside the female's body.

items.q: Which cell or structure is responsible for exchanging food, oxygen and wastes between mother and foetus?
items.e: Placenta: exchanging food, oxygen and wastes between mother and foetus.

items.q: Which animal has a “baby” stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Human life cycle: baby → child → teenager → adult.

items.q: Which animals change from a water-living young to a land-living adult?
items.e: Life cycles differ between groups of animals.

items.q: Which animals lay jelly-covered eggs in water; the young live in water and breathe with gills?
items.e: Life cycles differ between groups of animals.

items.q: A human's life cycle is typical of which group?
items.e: A human is a mammal.

items.q: A chicken lays eggs with hard shells that hatch in a nest. This is …
items.e: The egg develops outside the mother's body.

items.q: Some sharks keep their eggs inside the body until they hatch. This is …
items.e: The young feed on the yolk and are born alive.

items.q: Which animal has a “young dog” stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Dog life cycle: puppy → young dog → adult dog → old dog.

items.q: A dog's life cycle is typical of which group?
items.e: A dog is a mammal.

items.q: Which animal has a “child” stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Human life cycle: baby → child → teenager → adult.

items.q: What is ovovivipary?
c: the embryo is fed through a placenta
eggs are laid in a nest
the eggs are fertilised outside the body
eggs are kept inside the mother and hatch there; the young are born alive
items.e: Some sharks and snakes are ovoviviparous: the embryo feeds on the yolk.

items.q: A dog gives birth to puppies that were fed through a placenta. This is …
items.e: The placenta passes food and oxygen to the embryos.

items.q: Which animals give birth to live young and feed them milk?
items.e: Life cycles differ between groups of animals.

items.q: A chicken's life cycle is typical of which group?
items.e: A chicken is a bird.

items.q: What is vivipary?
c: the embryo develops inside the mother and is fed through a placenta; live young are born
eggs that hatch inside the mother without a placenta
items.e: Most mammals are viviparous.

items.q: Which animal has a “young chicken” stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Chicken life cycle: egg → chick → young chicken → adult hen.

items.q: Which animal has a “larva” stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Ladybird life cycle: egg → larva → pupa → adult ladybird.

items.q: What is ovipary?
c: eggs that hatch inside the mother
laying eggs that develop and hatch outside the mother's body
giving birth to live young fed by a placenta
items.e: Birds, most reptiles, fish and amphibians are oviparous.

items.q: Which animals lay eggs with hard shells and keep them warm?
items.e: Life cycles differ between groups of animals.

items.q: A frog's life cycle is typical of which group?
items.e: A frog is an amphibian.

items.q: Why do bird embryos need a lot of yolk but mammal embryos do not?
c: bird embryos grow inside the mother
mammal embryos do not need food
a mammal embryo gets food from the mother through the placenta
items.e: The placenta replaces the need for a large yolk store.

items.q: Which shows the life cycle of a mealworm beetle in the correct order?
items.e: Start with the egg and end with the adult.

items.q: What is a young frog that lives in water called?
items.e: Tadpoles have tails and gills.

items.q: What does the yolk sac do?
c: it stores food for the developing embryo
items.e: The yolk is rich in protein and fat.

items.q: What is an amniotic egg?
c: a jelly-covered egg laid in water
an egg that is fertilised outside the body
an egg with a shell and membranes (such as the amnion) that keep the embryo moist on land
items.e: Reptiles and birds lay amniotic eggs.

items.q: Which of these animals has a nymph stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Cockroach: egg → nymph → adult cockroach.

items.q: What is the stage of a butterfly between the caterpillar and the adult?
items.e: Inside the pupa, the caterpillar changes into a butterfly.

items.q: What is a life cycle?
c: the stages an animal goes through from egg or birth to adult
items.e: The adult then reproduces and the cycle starts again.

items.q: Which shows the life cycle of a mosquito in the correct order?
items.e: Start with the egg and end with the adult.

items.q: Why is the shell of a bird's egg porous?
c: so that oxygen can diffuse in and carbon dioxide out
so that water can flow in
so that the yolk can leave
items.e: The embryo needs oxygen for respiration.

items.q: Which of these animals has a tadpole stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Frog: egg → tadpole → young frog → adult frog.

items.q: Which animal has a three-stage life cycle?
items.e: Egg → nymph → adult.

items.q: What does the amnion do?
c: it stores food for the embryo
it exchanges gases through the shell
it surrounds the embryo with fluid that protects it from drying out and from shocks
items.e: The amniotic fluid acts as a cushion and keeps the embryo moist.

items.q: Which of these animals has a pupa stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Butterfly: egg → caterpillar (larva) → pupa → adult butterfly.

items.q: Which stage comes first in the life cycle of most animals?
items.e: Many animals start life as an egg.

items.q: Which animal has a four-stage life cycle?
items.e: Egg → larva → pupa → adult.

items.q: What does the allantois do in a bird's egg?
c: it stores wastes and helps with gaseous exchange
items.e: The allantois also carries blood vessels close to the shell.

items.q: Which shows the life cycle of a frog in the correct order?
c: egg → tadpole → young frog → adult frog
adult frog → young frog → tadpole → egg
tadpole → egg → young frog → adult frog
egg → young frog → tadpole → adult frog
items.e: Start with the egg and end with the adult.

items.q: Which of these animals has a larva stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Mosquito: egg → larva → pupa → adult mosquito.

items.q: Which of these animals has a pupa stage in its life cycle?
items.e: Mealworm beetle: egg → larva (mealworm) → pupa → adult beetle.

items.q: Which shows the life cycle of a butterfly in the correct order?
items.e: Start with the egg and end with the adult.

items.q: Which is an example of parental care?
c: a turtle burying eggs on a beach and leaving
a bird incubating its eggs and feeding its chicks
a frog laying eggs in a pond and swimming away
a fish laying millions of eggs and leaving
items.e: Parental care includes incubation, feeding and protection.

items.q: 20 snails are caught, marked and released. Later 75 are caught and 15 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
What are altricial young?
c: young that can run soon after birth
young that feed themselves at once
young that are born helpless, often blind and without feathers or fur, and need parental care
items.e: Kittens, puppies and many songbirds are altricial.

items.q: 80 grasshoppers are caught, marked and released. Later 75 are caught and 2 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
60 voles are caught, marked and released. Later 40 are caught and 2 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
Why do animals that give a lot of parental care produce fewer young?
c: they live only a short time
each young has a better chance of survival, so fewer are needed
their eggs are fertilised outside the body
items.e: Energy is put into caring for a few young rather than making many.

items.q: 20 fish are caught, marked and released. Later 30 are caught and 10 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
30 snails are caught, marked and released. Later 25 are caught and 12 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
80 voles are caught, marked and released. Later 75 are caught and 6 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
A springbok calf runs with the herd within hours of birth. It is …
items.e: Running soon after birth helps it escape predators.

items.q: What is the effect of predators on prey populations?
c: they always wipe out the prey
they keep prey numbers under control and help maintain species diversity
items.e: Biological control uses this.

items.q: A turtle lays about 100 eggs in the sand and leaves. What do you expect?
c: only a few hatchlings survive to adulthood
the eggs hatch inside the turtle
the mother returns to feed them
items.e: Many eggs and no parental care mean high losses.

items.q: Newly hatched sparrows are blind and naked and are fed by their parents. They are …
items.e: Altricial young need a lot of parental care.

items.q: 80 grasshoppers are caught, marked and released. Later 50 are caught and 3 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
45 woodlice are caught, marked and released. Later 75 are caught and 6 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
20 grasshoppers are caught, marked and released. Later 40 are caught and 12 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
20 fish are caught, marked and released. Later 50 are caught and 12 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
30 snails are caught, marked and released. Later 75 are caught and 3 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
What are precocial young?
c: young that hatch from eggs inside the mother
young that never leave the nest
young that are well developed at birth, with eyes open, and can move and feed soon
young that are born blind and helpless
items.e: Ducklings, chicks and antelope calves are precocial.

items.q: 45 beetles are caught, marked and released. Later 40 are caught and 4 of these are marked. Estimate the population size.
Musa grew sunflowers with different hours of light per day. Which condition gave the tallest plants?
items.e: Read the tallest bar.

items.q: Lwazi studies a plant structure: acorns that squirrels bury and forget. How does it help the plant reproduce?
c: They get planted in new places by animals.
They attract hummingbirds that carry pollen.
They make the plant look nice for people.
They attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.
items.e: Plant structures help with pollination or seed dispersal.

items.q: A flower has large, brightly coloured petals. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.q: Kyle studies a plant structure: flowers that open at night and smell strong. How does it help the plant reproduce?
c: They attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.
They let the wind carry seeds far away.
They make the plant look nice for people.
They attract moths and bats as pollinators.
items.e: Plant structures help with pollination or seed dispersal.

items.q: A flower has sticky or spiky pollen grains. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.q: A flower has anthers and stigma inside the flower. How is it most likely pollinated?
items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

c: They release pollen that the wind carries to other plants.

They make the plant look nice for people.
items.e: Plant structures help with pollination or seed dispersal.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.e: Read the tallest bar.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.e: Insect-pollinated flowers attract insects; wind-pollinated flowers release and catch pollen in the air.

items.e: Pollination moves pollen; dispersal moves seeds.
